Senses.Note: Sengzhao’s attributed line places a treasure within the mountain of form. Feiyin compares it with Xuedou’s deliberate reversal of where the treasure hangs. Tianyin asks the assembly whether it has taken what the saying names. Senses.Explanation: The Middle Way is the course between or beyond opposed extremes. Yongming Yanshou’s compiled treatise says to proceed directly toward it; Baozhi’s verse says not to cling either to the two sides or to the Middle Way itself. Baizhang Huaihai makes the sharper Chan move: in a long inventory of learned attainments, even learning emptiness, equality, and the Middle Way can become an affliction when grasped as acquired understanding.

Senses.PreferredTarget: bright and numinous
Senses.Note: The phrase also appears in first-person retrospective description. One unnamed interlocutor says he was still "hazy and indistinct, bright and numinous, and had not yet obtained stability" (恍恍惚惚、昭昭靈靈，也未得個安穩); a later account says that this bright-and-numinous condition could not be made to arise and could not be found after a subsequent event. A verse asks, "what is the bright and numinous? By the time you blink, it has already been missed" (昭昭靈靈是什麼？眨得眼來已蹉過). Productive forms include "the bright-and-numinous one" (the nominal “bright-and-numinous one” form, 14 occurrences in 12 texts) and "recognize the bright and numinous" (認昭昭靈靈, 21 in 16). Eight texts preserve the sleep challenge's wording "the bright and numinous is your reality" (昭昭靈靈是汝真實).

Senses.Explanation: A reduplicated description: brightly evident (昭昭) and keenly numinous or responsive (靈靈), hence "bright and numinous." It is attested. Chinese Chan records frequently use the phrase while rejecting its identification with one's true self. One address asks, "if you recognize the bright and numinous as your reality, why does it no longer remain bright and numinous when you are asleep?" (汝若認昭昭靈靈是汝真實，為甚麼瞌睡時又不成昭昭靈靈). The same address gives a direct account: the bright and numinous arises because colors, sounds, scents, and other things before one are distinguished; without those things it is like "turtle fur and rabbit horns" (昭昭靈靈，祇因前塵色聲香等法而有分別；若無前塵，同於龜毛兔角). Another record states that the fault lies in taking the presently bright and numinous as correct, since it "arises dependent on encountered objects" (昭昭靈靈乃是緣境而有). These are the corpus's explicit predicates, not an entry-level theory of consciousness.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1420.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chushi Fanqi. Chushi Fanqi gives a short hall address full of deliberately impossible images: fetching fire from the deep sea, catching fish on a high peak, and making a wooden man open a bowl. He tells his hearers not to sigh, then closes that turn by saying that contention never yields enough while yielding leaves more than enough. The proverb is Chushi's present voice here, before a separate Flower Garland scripture gathering begins in the record.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB163.xml). Selected Record of Chan Master Guting’s Sayings. Guting Shanjian raises a case in which a monk asks Jiashan and then Shishuang about brushing away dust to see Buddha; the two teachers answer differently, and Jiashan boasts that his handling of the doorway surpasses Shishuang's. Guting asks whether the difference really amounts to a hundred paces, gives the proverb about contention and yielding as his own appraisal, and invites other teachers to examine it. The saying moderates a rivalry over who handled the case better; it is not speech by either teacher in the old case.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB186.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Linyexi. At the opening of his teaching hall, Linye Tongqi lifts a robe and says that what his late teacher used remains inexhaustible. He adds that trying to contend for it would not suffice, while yielding it leaves abundance, then puts on the robe and ascends the seat to offer incense. The phrase is Linye's present ceremonial response to receiving a teaching inheritance, rather than a literal dispute over ownership of the garment.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. At an evening instruction prompted by a land dispute involving the Ding family, Tian'an Sheng asks the assembly to respond to his verse about an ancestral plot left overgrown and people creating a quarrel at the mountain gate. A monk named Zhan offers a different maxim, but Tian'an rejects it and supplies his own answers, including the line that contention is insufficient and yielding leaves more than enough. Here the proverb directly counsels restraint in the property quarrel; Tian'an, not the monk, voices it.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB249.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fangrongxi. Fangrong Ruxi first cites an old saying about giving a staff to someone who has one and taking it from someone who lacks one. He says it resembles the proverb about contention and yielding, but then sets giving, taking, having and lacking aside and asks what a staff is. After a pause he strikes the staff and closes the turn. The old staff saying belongs to an unnamed earlier voice; the proverb and challenge are Fangrong's present commentary.

Hongzhi Zhengjue raises an old exchange: Snowpeak says that a group of monkeys each carries an ancient mirror, and Sansheng challenges the name and then Snowpeak's response. Hongzhi says that if he had heard Snowpeak say a flaw had appeared, he would have stepped forward with an acknowledgment. Asked why, he closes with the proverb about contention and yielding. Hongzhi is applying the line to his imagined handling of the inherited case, not reporting it as Snowpeak's speech.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1420.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chushi Fanqi. Chushi Fanqi gives a short hall address full of deliberately impossible images: fetching fire from the deep sea, catching fish on a high peak, and making a wooden man open a bowl. He tells his hearers not to sigh, then closes that turn by saying that contention never yields enough while yielding leaves more than enough. The proverb is Chushi's present voice here, before a separate Flower Garland scripture gathering begins in the record.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB163.xml). Selected Record of Chan Master Guting’s Sayings. Guting Shanjian raises a case in which a monk asks Jiashan and then Shishuang about brushing away dust to see Buddha; the two teachers answer differently, and Jiashan boasts that his handling of the doorway surpasses Shishuang's. Guting asks whether the difference really amounts to a hundred paces, gives the proverb about contention and yielding as his own appraisal, and invites other teachers to examine it. The saying moderates a rivalry over who handled the case better; it is not speech by either teacher in the old case.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB186.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Linyexi. At the opening of his teaching hall, Linye Tongqi lifts a robe and says that what his late teacher used remains inexhaustible. He adds that trying to contend for it would not suffice, while yielding it leaves abundance, then puts on the robe and ascends the seat to offer incense. The phrase is Linye's present ceremonial response to receiving a teaching inheritance, rather than a literal dispute over ownership of the garment.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. At an evening instruction prompted by a land dispute involving the Ding family, Tian'an Sheng asks the assembly to respond to his verse about an ancestral plot left overgrown and people creating a quarrel at the mountain gate. A monk named Zhan offers a different maxim, but Tian'an rejects it and supplies his own answers, including the line that contention is insufficient and yielding leaves more than enough. Here the proverb directly counsels restraint in the property quarrel; Tian'an, not the monk, voices it.

Senses.Explanation: The proverb says that fighting for a share still leaves too little, while yielding leaves abundance. The six masters apply it to a quarrel, inherited teaching, rival readings of old cases and a present challenge about a staff. Chushi Fanqi gives a short hall address full of deliberately impossible images: fetching fire from the deep sea, catching fish on a high peak, and making a wooden man open a bowl. He tells his hearers not to sigh, then closes that turn by saying that contention never yields enough while yielding leaves more than enough. The proverb is Chushi's present voice here, before a separate Flower Garland scripture gathering begins in the record. Guting Shanjian raises a case in which a monk asks Jiashan and then Shishuang about brushing away dust to see Buddha; the two teachers answer differently, and Jiashan boasts that his handling of the doorway surpasses Shishuang's. Guting asks whether the difference really amounts to a hundred paces, gives the proverb about contention and yielding as his own appraisal, and invites other teachers to examine it. The saying moderates a rivalry over who handled the case better; it is not speech by either teacher in the old case. At the opening of his teaching hall, Linye Tongqi lifts a robe and says that what his late teacher used remains inexhaustible. He adds that trying to contend for it would not suffice, while yielding it leaves abundance, then puts on the robe and ascends the seat to offer incense. The phrase is Linye's present ceremonial response to receiving a teaching inheritance, rather than a literal dispute over ownership of the garment. At an evening instruction prompted by a land dispute involving the Ding family, Tian'an Sheng asks the assembly to respond to his verse about an ancestral plot left overgrown and people creating a quarrel at the mountain gate. A monk named Zhan offers a different maxim, but Tian'an rejects it and supplies his own answers, including the line that contention is insufficient and yielding leaves more than enough. Here the proverb directly counsels restraint in the property quarrel; Tian'an, not the monk, voices it. Fangrong Ruxi first cites an old saying about giving a staff to someone who has one and taking it from someone who lacks one. He says it resembles the proverb about contention and yielding, but then sets giving, taking, having and lacking aside and asks what a staff is. After a pause he strikes the staff and closes the turn. The old staff saying belongs to an unnamed earlier voice; the proverb and challenge are Fangrong's present commentary. Hongzhi Zhengjue raises an old exchange: Snowpeak says that a group of monkeys each carries an ancient mirror, and Sansheng challenges the name and then Snowpeak's response. Hongzhi says that if he had heard Snowpeak say a flaw had appeared, he would have stepped forward with an acknowledgment. Asked why, he closes with the proverb about contention and yielding. Hongzhi is applying the line to his imagined handling of the inherited case, not reporting it as Snowpeak's speech.

Yongjia true aspect direct entry verse
Senses.Note: Yongjia's longer verse first likens reward sought through attachment to forms to an arrow shot upward that must fall when its force runs out. This pair offers the gate of unconditioned true aspect instead. Pu'an insists on holding appearance and its basis together; Feiyin asks what the gate is; Daxiu warns against using the language of freedom to excuse harm. Yuanwu links the pair to sudden awakening, Fachang revoices it after a verse on worldly achievement, and Cishou explains it in relation to present conduct. The last clause has a separate public article; this complete pair retains the contrast with the gate and its later tests.

Occurrences.Kwic: 人話墮，直饒口似秤槌，未免灯籠勘破。不知道絕功勳，妄自脩因證果，若逢臨濟、德山，應是難能放過。但知一念回心，定免三乘羈鎻。上堂云：青山鳥道，登者即迷。碧落無波，動犯風影。不是目前法，莫生種種心。明暗不相關，虗空無背面。到這裏，直似秋潭月影、靜夜鍾聲，猶是生死岸頭事，莫當等閑。不見古者道：直須向那邊擔荷了，却來這邊行李揩磨心識，盡却今時過患。直似枯木逢春不潤，始有少分相應。古人與麼說話意作麼生？那邊檐荷箇什麼？這邊又作麼生行李？除非久參碩德乃可知之。莫只與麼業識忙忙，無明人我私心作解，妄生穿鑿，如磨塼作鏡相似，多少謷訛？快須著力，莫待前頭路盡方始著忙。一朝心眼頓開，方知法昌老以佛法為事。上堂，云：昨日送殘年，今朝賀新歲，新歲與殘年，相逐如流水。人無百年人，盡作千年累，一箇無常身，百端生狡計。殺命資口腹，結業求富貴，片善不曾修，日為煩惱醉。且莫醉，起來共你說些：周秦并漢魏，覇業及圖王，文經兼武緯，凌煙閣上數如麻，盡向青山脚下排頭睡，爭似無為實相門，一超直入如來地。上堂云：年年四月十六，諸方盡皆禁足。法昌山裏如何？但見山青水淥。上堂，云：諸仁者！心是根，法是塵，兩種猶如鏡上痕，痕垢盡時光始現，心法雙忘性即真。古人已是四楞著地了也，汝等諸人作麼生會？內視不己見，返聽不我聞，覺體超然，不屬量數，正是痕垢在你。且道鏡在什麼處？直饒分明拈出，我更問你什麼處得來？你若不知來處，山僧為你指出：鍊得銅山沒一星，入紅爐裏又埃塵，須知本自圓成物，本自圓成無故新。勘辯勘辯師在雙嶺受請，與英、勝二首座相別，云：三年聚首，無事不知，檢點將來，不無滲漏。以拄杖劃一劃，云：這箇且止，宗門事作麼生？英云：須彌安鼻孔。師云：與麼則臨崖看虎眼，特地一場愁。英云：深沙努眼睛。師云：爭奈聖凡無異路，方便有多門？英云：鐵蛇鑽不入。師云：這般漢有甚共語處？英云：自緣根力淺，莫怨太陽春。却劃一劃，云：宗門事且止，這箇事作麼生？師便掌。英云：這漳州子莫無去就。師云：你這般見解，不打更待何時？又打。英云：也是老僧招得。英、勝二人到山相訪，英云：和尚尋常愛檢點諸方，今日為甚却來古庿裏作活計？師云：打草只要蛇驚。英云：且莫塗糊人好。師云：你又刺頭入膠盆作什麼？英云：古人道：我見兩箇泥牛鬪入海，所以住山。未審和尚見箇什麼？師云：你他時異

Occurrences.Kwic: ，強名曰一心。此一心靜時，亦無三界。只為眾生迷時三界有，悟去十方空。先聖不得已，有一言半句。如將黃葉作金錢，權止小兒啼哭。然雖如是，幾箇知音？吳國夫人有如是壽筭，有如是子孫，有如是宅舍，有如是富貴。以理推之，來源自有。更願夫人堅固道心，增修白業。直至成佛，方為究竟。教云：一切眾生具有如來智慧德相，但以妄想執著而不證得。於是稱法界性，說華嚴經。法界者，一切眾生真心之本體也。如是則一切眾生本來是佛。佛者以何為義？以覺為義。梵語佛陀，此番為覺。在迷底人分上，謂之背覺合塵。在悟底人分上，謂之背塵合覺。諸佛覺有三義：自覺、覺它、覺行圓滿。自覺者，勝凡夫。不覺覺它者，勝二乘。人只解自覺，不能覺它。覺行圓滿者，勝菩薩。菩薩雖修如上二覺，未能圓滿佛，謂之大圓滿覺。如中秋月，無幽不燭。初機之人，十二時中一箇覺字，觀照日久歲深，塵勞境界自然淡薄。永嘉云：覺即了，不施功，一切有為法不同。住相布施生天福，猶如仰箭射虗空。勢力盡，箭還墜，招得來生不如意。爭似無為實相門，一超直入如來地。如來地者，便是覺也。此是成佛作祖之捷徑，超生越死之路頭。三世諸佛共傳，六代祖師同說。願生深信，莫作等閑。不見肅宗帝問忠國師：時中如何用心修行？國師云：但能二六時中覺妄修真，如煉精金，光明轉熾。一切眾生癡迷不覺，從開眼至合眼，所作無非虗妄，何嘗覺悟來？你如今食前方丈，水陸畢陳，還覺宰殺物命麼？你居華堂大廈，還覺還當麼？你羅綺千箱，還覺衣不蓋身者麼？你鞭撻奴婢，還覺無慈悲麼？這裏若覺得快時，設使墮在地獄，亦須早出頭來。古人謂之：不愁念起，唯恐覺遲。起即是病，覺即是藥。常以此藥而治此病，如水救火，即時而滅。昔溈山問中邑和尚：如何是佛性義？邑云：我為你說箇喻。如一間屋，周回六窻，中間繫一獼猴，東窻喚東邊應，西窻喚西邊應，如是六󰈧俱喚，六窻俱應。溈山又問：忽然獼猴睡著時如何？邑下禪床擒住云：狌狌，我與你相見。諸有智者以譬喻得解。六窻者，六根門頭也。獼猴者，一精明性也。佛云：本是一精明，分為六和合。只是者箇獼猴時中合惺惺處，却不能了了地惺惺；時中□□□處，却不能齁󳶓地瞌睡。諸人若也未會，更聽□□：人人有箇老獼猴，暮四朝三卒未休。喚著便能□□處，八花碍上輥金毬。上堂□。宵燈燭鬪熒煌，幸馬縱橫徹曉忙，倒底不知燈是火，區區幾箇解回光？若論此

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 和尚不恁麼說，山僧亦不恁麼說。嗟哉！末法之人，信根淺薄，智力衰微，不肯刻苦參究，焉能徹法源底？或一年半載，略用功夫，以聰明見領，略一知半解，認著個主人公，逢人便喝。為師不下鉗錘，懡㦬放過，使野犴遍地，瞞昧人家男女，正是一盲引眾盲，相牽入火坑。若有法與人，名野犴鳴；說法無可說，名曰獅子吼。正是義中無句，句中無義，如五臺山上雲蒸飯。如此說，不妨熾然說。若以文字塞人天機，若以道理障人真智，非但不能為人天眼目，抱甕之流自了無暇。大眾！生死事大，各各扣己而參，一時一刻清淨，一時一刻是佛。然而清淨俱不執，何勞更問祖師禪？」說戒普說。「大眾！今夜羯磨，明日說戒，身三口四之愆尤，從頭發露俱消雪。所以道：『罪性本空猶心造，心若忘時罪亦忘，心忘罪滅兩皆空，是則名為真懺悔。』若忘心，自忘物，忘物則忘人，人物俱忘，看是何物？這裡識得破，善入戒體，去來本自在，真心任遍知。其或未然，古人道：『著相持戒生天福，猶如仰箭射虛空。勢力盡，箭還墜，招得來生不如意。爭似無為實相門，一超直入如來地。』有等外道聞恁麼說，他也道無為無為。末法當代，去聖時遙，如粵地天邊之所，無智人辨別，竟遞相聾瞽，瞎人眼目。又扯無為，無所不為，便縱行婬怒癡，廣肆殺害，亦曰無妨。罪過罪過。如山僧不涉世諦，遠離塵囂，心中亦無遠離之念，信口道來，不假思議，自然恰好。從朝至暮，覓絲毫生相不可得，覓絲毫滅相不可得，將不可得又不可得，又不妨應用于千差，此名無為，無所不為。山僧為諸人說破，當捨妄歸真。皈依佛。佛者，自性之覺體；皈依法，法者，一念心清淨。皈依僧，僧者，即自性之真體也。如此自心受持，不涉外緣，即不皈依邪魔外道。外道者，心外有法，名為外道。或見光見花、見佛、見菩薩、幢幡、寶蓋、童子來迎，俱是外道、魔王眷屬。在正教觀來，趁出法海邊外，永不聞佛法之名。何故？謗大般若。畢竟如何即是？我要你正不許邪，要你是不許非，要你上不許下。前有僧問山僧：『如何是向上事？』山僧向他道：『但莫向下。』語既如然，事事如然。大眾！粵地法道無聞，善知識難遇，當生慶幸，不可空過時光。努力今生須了卻，莫教永劫受餘殃。」下座。解制普說。師云：「龍牙道：『天下名山到因腳，辛苦多年與襪著。而今老大不能行，手裡把柄破木杓。』又五祖演道：『腳也不能著草鞋，手也不能把木杓，端坐受供養，施

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: ，豈不省要哉？玄沙一日見人𢱲屍過，指而示眾：四箇死漢𢱲一箇活漢，若隨情見，却是玄沙自相顛倒。若以向上正眼離見超情，乃知玄沙為人極是親切，是故透脫須出他陰界。不見古德道：白雲淡泞，水注滄溟，萬法本閑，而人自閙。果是真實諦當，聊聞舉著，便知落處，可以透脫生死，不在陰界中窒礙，如鳥出籠，自由自在。自餘一切機用言句，只一截便休，更不落第二見也。示照道人(尼)示照道人釋門奇特，徑截超證，速與般若相應，無出禪宗，此乃如來最上乘清淨禪也。自靈山拈花，金色頭陀微笑，迦文付授涅槃妙心正法眼藏，教外別行，單傳心印，歷代四七。至達磨西來，直指人心，見性成佛，無論凡聖久近，但根器相投，一念透脫，更不假三僧祇劫，便證本來圓成淨妙調御。是故游泳此宗，資大法器，從初立志跂步，便要超卓，所謂立地成佛。蹔時斂念，便證無生，不立前後際，不從他得，惟是自己分上猛利操修。如斬一綟絲，一斬一切斬，性靈瞥脫，前念是凡，後念是聖，擬不擬凡聖一如，含吐十虗，更無方所。永嘉道：爭似無為實相門，一超直入如來地。法華會上龍女獻一珠即成正覺，豈非轉念便證妙果耶？蓋此法天地不能覆載、虗空不可包容，蘊在一切含靈根脚、為一切依倚，長時淨倮倮無處不周，但為情識所拘、聞見所隔，妄認緣影為心、四大為身，不能證得此正體，所以諸聖以悲願力指出示人，令一切群生有根器者回光返照、單拈獨證去。只如龍女所獻之寶即今在甚處？若纔舉著，便和坐子承當得，終不向語言中作解會、心機意想裏作窠窟，便與靈山無垢世界無二無別也。從上來唯貴最初一念、最初一句，念未生、聲未發，直下截斷，千聖靈機、萬靈印契一時劃破，可不是脫灑自由、得大自在要妙處耶？龐居士問馬大師：不與萬法為侶是什麼人？馬師云：待汝一口吸盡西江水即向汝道。此箇公案多有涉唇吻商量、作機境解會，殊不稟宗猷也。要須是箇生鐵鑄就底，方能逆流超證，乃解翻却二老鐵船，始到壁立萬仞處，方知無許多事。示倫上人示倫上人一切有心，天地懸隔，酌然如今透關不得，只為心多執重。若脫然摒當到無心之地，一切妄染情習俱盡，知見解礙都銷，更有甚事？是故南泉云：平常心是道。然纔起念，待要平常，早乖差了也。此最為微細難湊處，沒量大人到箇裏踟蹰，何況學地？直須抵死謾生，咬嚼教斷，直似大死底人，絕氣息然後甦醒，始知廓同太虗，方到脚蹋實地。深證此事，明得

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 人話墮，直饒口似秤槌，未免灯籠勘破。不知道絕功勳，妄自脩因證果，若逢臨濟、德山，應是難能放過。但知一念回心，定免三乘羈鎻。上堂云：青山鳥道，登者即迷。碧落無波，動犯風影。不是目前法，莫生種種心。明暗不相關，虗空無背面。到這裏，直似秋潭月影、靜夜鍾聲，猶是生死岸頭事，莫當等閑。不見古者道：直須向那邊擔荷了，却來這邊行李揩磨心識，盡却今時過患。直似枯木逢春不潤，始有少分相應。古人與麼說話意作麼生？那邊檐荷箇什麼？這邊又作麼生行李？除非久參碩德乃可知之。莫只與麼業識忙忙，無明人我私心作解，妄生穿鑿，如磨塼作鏡相似，多少謷訛？快須著力，莫待前頭路盡方始著忙。一朝心眼頓開，方知法昌老以佛法為事。上堂，云：昨日送殘年，今朝賀新歲，新歲與殘年，相逐如流水。人無百年人，盡作千年累，一箇無常身，百端生狡計。殺命資口腹，結業求富貴，片善不曾修，日為煩惱醉。且莫醉，起來共你說些：周秦并漢魏，覇業及圖王，文經兼武緯，凌煙閣上數如麻，盡向青山脚下排頭睡，爭似無為實相門，一超直入如來地。上堂云：年年四月十六，諸方盡皆禁足。法昌山裏如何？但見山青水淥。上堂，云：諸仁者！心是根，法是塵，兩種猶如鏡上痕，痕垢盡時光始現，心法雙忘性即真。古人已是四楞著地了也，汝等諸人作麼生會？內視不己見，返聽不我聞，覺體超然，不屬量數，正是痕垢在你。且道鏡在什麼處？直饒分明拈出，我更問你什麼處得來？你若不知來處，山僧為你指出：鍊得銅山沒一星，入紅爐裏又埃塵，須知本自圓成物，本自圓成無故新。勘辯勘辯師在雙嶺受請，與英、勝二首座相別，云：三年聚首，無事不知，檢點將來，不無滲漏。以拄杖劃一劃，云：這箇且止，宗門事作麼生？英云：須彌安鼻孔。師云：與麼則臨崖看虎眼，特地一場愁。英云：深沙努眼睛。師云：爭奈聖凡無異路，方便有多門？英云：鐵蛇鑽不入。師云：這般漢有甚共語處？英云：自緣根力淺，莫怨太陽春。却劃一劃，云：宗門事且止，這箇事作麼生？師便掌。英云：這漳州子莫無去就。師云：你這般見解，不打更待何時？又打。英云：也是老僧招得。英、勝二人到山相訪，英云：和尚尋常愛檢點諸方，今日為甚却來古庿裏作活計？師云：打草只要蛇驚。英云：且莫塗糊人好。師云：你又刺頭入膠盆作什麼？英云：古人道：我見兩箇泥牛鬪入海，所以住山。未審和尚見箇什麼？師云：你他時異

ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 爭似無為實相門，一超直入如來地

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: ，強名曰一心。此一心靜時，亦無三界。只為眾生迷時三界有，悟去十方空。先聖不得已，有一言半句。如將黃葉作金錢，權止小兒啼哭。然雖如是，幾箇知音？吳國夫人有如是壽筭，有如是子孫，有如是宅舍，有如是富貴。以理推之，來源自有。更願夫人堅固道心，增修白業。直至成佛，方為究竟。教云：一切眾生具有如來智慧德相，但以妄想執著而不證得。於是稱法界性，說華嚴經。法界者，一切眾生真心之本體也。如是則一切眾生本來是佛。佛者以何為義？以覺為義。梵語佛陀，此番為覺。在迷底人分上，謂之背覺合塵。在悟底人分上，謂之背塵合覺。諸佛覺有三義：自覺、覺它、覺行圓滿。自覺者，勝凡夫。不覺覺它者，勝二乘。人只解自覺，不能覺它。覺行圓滿者，勝菩薩。菩薩雖修如上二覺，未能圓滿佛，謂之大圓滿覺。如中秋月，無幽不燭。初機之人，十二時中一箇覺字，觀照日久歲深，塵勞境界自然淡薄。永嘉云：覺即了，不施功，一切有為法不同。住相布施生天福，猶如仰箭射虗空。勢力盡，箭還墜，招得來生不如意。爭似無為實相門，一超直入如來地。如來地者，便是覺也。此是成佛作祖之捷徑，超生越死之路頭。三世諸佛共傳，六代祖師同說。願生深信，莫作等閑。不見肅宗帝問忠國師：時中如何用心修行？國師云：但能二六時中覺妄修真，如煉精金，光明轉熾。一切眾生癡迷不覺，從開眼至合眼，所作無非虗妄，何嘗覺悟來？你如今食前方丈，水陸畢陳，還覺宰殺物命麼？你居華堂大廈，還覺還當麼？你羅綺千箱，還覺衣不蓋身者麼？你鞭撻奴婢，還覺無慈悲麼？這裏若覺得快時，設使墮在地獄，亦須早出頭來。古人謂之：不愁念起，唯恐覺遲。起即是病，覺即是藥。常以此藥而治此病，如水救火，即時而滅。昔溈山問中邑和尚：如何是佛性義？邑云：我為你說箇喻。如一間屋，周回六窻，中間繫一獼猴，東窻喚東邊應，西窻喚西邊應，如是六󰈧俱喚，六窻俱應。溈山又問：忽然獼猴睡著時如何？邑下禪床擒住云：狌狌，我與你相見。諸有智者以譬喻得解。六窻者，六根門頭也。獼猴者，一精明性也。佛云：本是一精明，分為六和合。只是者箇獼猴時中合惺惺處，却不能了了地惺惺；時中□□□處，却不能齁󳶓地瞌睡。諸人若也未會，更聽□□：人人有箇老獼猴，暮四朝三卒未休。喚著便能□□處，八花碍上輥金毬。上堂□。宵燈燭鬪熒煌，幸馬縱橫徹曉忙，倒底不知燈是火，區區幾箇解回光？若論此

ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 爭似無為實相門，一超直入如來地

Senses.Explanation: Yongjia contrasts a reward that expires with direct entry through the gate of true aspect. The complete verse's arrow image sets up this pair as an alternative to merit sought through attachment. Six later works apply the pair to offerings, conduct, awakening, and worldly success.

Senses.PreferredTarget: how could you know how to draw a bow and shoot Yuchi?
SearchAliases: how could you draw a bow against Yuchi?
who knows how to shoot Yuchi?
Senses.Explanation: A martial challenge denying that an unproved speaker knows how to draw the bow against the formidable Yuchi. Tian'an Sheng and Baichi Xingyuan answer monks with the line after comparing them to Jinya. Yinyuan Longqi, Yuan'an Liao, and Mingjue Cong use the same challenge in separate public exchanges, with local variants such as “know,” “suppose,” and “think” in the companion clause.
Senses.Note: The Yuchi line remains the stable challenge while the preceding Jinya clause varies. Lamp recensions and passive repetitions of the old Shaoshan exchange are excluded because direct recorded-sayings uses meet the evidence floor.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「是真語，是如語。」進云：「今日和尚登曲彔床，又舉揚何事？」師云：「不異語。」進云：「不須重說偈言。」便禮拜歸眾，師云：「孟八郎漢卻恁麼去也。」問：「一句了然超百億，如何今日又重宣？」師云：「為著阿誰？」進云：「恁麼則杖頭有眼分明在也。」師云：「做出便見。」問：「金牛飯、趙州茶，只為饑渴者，秪如不饑不渴底人來作麼生接待？」師打云：「也少你這一頓不得。」進云：「恁麼則一眾飽餐去也。」師云：「且道是何滋味？」僧便喝，師又打。問：「釋迦、彌勒猶是他奴，畢竟他是阿誰？」師云：「不識。」進云：「若然，則大千沙界任縱橫也。」師云：「且道他是阿誰？」僧喝，師打云：「鄭州出曹門。」問：「目前無法，意在目前。如何是目前法？」師打，云：「棒頭有眼。」進云：「因甚隱隱猶懷舊日嫌？」師云：「蒼天，蒼天。」進云：「莫把是非來入耳，從前知己反為讎。」師云：「自知較一半。」師乃云：「若論本分提綱，盡十方界無有針鋒許不是當人真實之體，有甚根塵器界、罪行福行而不一切智智清淨？古人道箇『眾罪如霜露，慧日能消除。』已屬剩語，此外更有所說，何異捏目生花？事不獲已，與汝箇真實指注。」驀豎拂子，云：「看，看！只這箇，名不得、狀不得、聖凡他不得、是非他不得，除是絕羅籠、出窠臼底衲僧向威音那畔一逴逴得，便轉向今世門頭大行闊步，便恁麼去，魔宮佛國任性逍遙，地獄天堂隨緣放曠，自然綽綽然有餘裕。

Senses.Explanation: Zhengzhou leaving by Cao Gate is the records' image for going conspicuously off course. Zhongfeng Mingben applies it to practice that falls far short of the old masters; Yushan Shangsi uses it as a rebuke, and Dahui Zonggao uses it in two separate addresses to reject proposed understandings. Jingshan Xiu likewise says competing explanations take this wrong route. The expression judges the approach as badly misplaced rather than naming an actual journey.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (D/D48/D48n8939.xml). Recorded Sayings of Ancient Venerable Masters, Wuzu Fayan's own section, where he names himself Fayan touring over ten years among the venerables. Wuzu Fayan owns the originating deployment: on his entry day he raises the Patriarch Bodhidharma's transmission verse, adds that Damo came trusting his feet and spoke trusting his mouth while late descendants all turned it into calculation, and to meet the place of flowering and fruiting gives the Zhengzhou pears, Qingzhou dates, nothing surpassing a good source.

Occurrences.Kwic: 復舉：祖師云：吾本來此土，傳法救迷情，一華開五葉，結果自然成。五祖法演和尚云：達磨大師信脚來，信口道，後代兒孫多成計較。諸人要會開華結果處麼？鄭州梨，青州棗，萬物無過出處好。師云：提本分鉗鎚，碎情解窠窟，還他五祖老人要見開華結果處則大遠在。諸人要會開華結果處麼？拈却鄭州梨，放下青州棗，出門便是長安道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1414.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liao'an Qingyu. Liao'an Qingyu owns the reprise deployment: after raising Wuzu Fayan's gloss on the transmission verse he comments with the intrinsic-implement hammer crushing the nest of conceptual understanding, grants that Old Wuzu's wish to see the flowering-and-fruiting place is still far off, and tells them to meet it thus — put down the Zhengzhou pears and Qingzhou dates, and out the door is the Chang'an road.

Occurrences.Kwic: 為青州佛實舉火云：「鄭州梨、青州棗，萬物無過出處好。實禪人還知麼？若知出處，便解當處出生、隨處滅盡，不見有生死去來之相，從來寸步未嘗移，那涉山東與山西？若猶未知……」攛火炬云：「老僧助汝一把火，炤徹面門離處所。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J10/J10nA158.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun. Miyun Yuanwu owns the funeral deployment: at monk Qingzhou Foshi's cremation he offers the pears-and-dates line, asks whether Foshi knows the source, and if he knows it he is equipped to be born on the spot and vanish wherever, never having moved an inch, never mind Shandong or Shanxi.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. Senses.Explanation: Putting another head atop one's head means adding a needless construction to what is already present. Huishan Jiexian applies it to turning expedient training procedures into a fixed method, pairing it with speaking of a dream inside a dream. Yikui Yuankui uses it when the forms before the assembly are additionally called Buddha. Yinyuan Longqi makes the naming problem explicit: calling the raised staff a staff adds a head, but refusing the name seeks life apart from the head. Shengke Deyu gives the phrase as his answer to 'what is Buddha?' and sets it against 'cut off the head to seek life.' A lamp recension of Linji Yixuan supplies the pointed question behind the image: after seekers add what is unnecessary, what do they lack?

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1360.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Xiatang Huiyuan. Xiatang Huiyuan tells listeners that finding an entrance is insufficient: they must also find a way out. He says learning Chan is easy but getting free of Chan is difficult, and rejects making patterns to imitate. He then speaks of fixing the whole expanse with a single seal and of cold and heat reaching everywhere. Turning this claim into a question, he says that sky is above the head and earth beneath the feet, with the two eyes balanced like equal weights, and asks how the listeners will apply that seal. He shouts and adds the image of a headless boat going down to Yangzhou. The pair is Xiatang’s present challenge, not a quotation assigned to an ancient. It brings his vast account of the seal back to the listener’s immediate position without supplying a procedure for sealing it.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1414.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liao’an Qingyu. Liao'an Qingyu opens a hall address with sky above the head and earth below the feet, adding that the compass directions retain their usual places. He then makes the scene extravagant: the world mountain rises in the middle, treasures shine, something falls when released and rises when supported, and a night market opens on a tiny insect’s eyelash. He closes with the old foreign patriarch escaping with one shoe and a shout. The stable orientation therefore opens a performance of reversal and disproportion rather than a geography lesson. Liao'an himself voices the pair in the current address. The passage gives no separate interlocutor’s question and does not explain each fantastic image as a fixed doctrine; the one-shoe departure is part of his poetic address, not evidence of a newly reported historical event.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1419.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuansou Xingduan. Yuansou Xingduan raises the case in which Nanquan throws a tile toward a monk, the monk turns, and Nanquan raises a foot. The monk cannot answer and later asks whether the thrown tile was meant to awaken him; Nanquan asks what the raised foot meant, and the monk is again silent. Yuansou compares an unexpected precious jewel thrown in the dark to something that makes its recipient reach for a sword. He says Nanquan has lost an eye and asks what the matter finally comes to. His present answer begins with sky above the head and earth below the feet, then joins a sweet-melon vine bearing a bitter gourd to Shakyamuni not receiving Dipankara’s prediction. Thus Nanquan and the monk belong to the raised case; Yuansou is the speaker of the exact pair. Ordinary orientation and incongruous continuations form his critical cap, without settling the tile and foot into a simple explanation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雲散碧天寬。蓮宮佛剎花無數，眨起眉毛子細觀。師云：觀則不無，喚什麼作一物？喝一喝。上堂，舉：仰山到東寺，寺問：汝是什麼處人？山云：廣南人。寺云：我聞廣南有鎮海明珠，是否？山云：是。寺云：此珠如何？山云：白月即隱，黑月即現。寺云：還將得來麼？山云：將得來。寺云：何不呈似老僧？山叉手近前云：昨到溈山，被索此珠，直得無言可對，無理可伸。寺云：真師子兒！善師子吼！師云：仰山雖是箇師子兒，爭奈把鎮海明珠作豌豆賣却，千古之下遭人點檢。山僧今日黨理不黨親，便是東寺到來，也須勘過了打。上堂：頭上是天，脚下是地。青山是青山，白雲是白雲。你會也，有馬騎馬，無馬步行。你若不會，夜行莫踏白。不是水，定是石。上堂：山門頭合掌，佛殿裏燒香。且道有指示無指示？劍去久矣，爾方刻舟。除夜，小參。僧問：一年將盡夜，萬里未歸人，還許歸去也無？師云：十里長亭，五里短亭。進云：與麼則不歸也。師云：直須歸去。進云：作麼生是到家一句？師云：天寒日短，兩人共一椀。乃云：作一句商量，師子吼、野干鳴；不作一句商量，野干鳴、師子吼。一時坐斷，未許作家；千里持來，堪作何用？盡乾坤大地無不說老婆禪，爭知永祚這裏不打這鼓笛
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1420.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chushi Fanqi. Chushi Fanqi gives a short hall address beginning with sky above the head and earth beneath the feet. He continues that green mountains are green mountains and white clouds are white clouds. If the listeners understand, they can ride when they have a horse and walk when they do not; if they do not, he warns them not to step on a pale patch while travelling at night, since it may be water or stone. Chushi himself speaks throughout this address, which follows a separate raised case and precedes another hall turn. The pair introduces ordinary recognition and practical response, while the night-travel warning prevents the apparently obvious language from becoming a claim that every situation has already been understood. No hidden meaning for each mountain or cloud is specified.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Above the head, a boundless expanse; beneath the feet, a boundless expanse.
AlternateTargets: Vast and open overhead, vast and open underfoot.
SearchAliases: vast overhead vast beneath feet Chan
above head below feet boundless Zen
Senses.Note: Poshan gives it as an answer to one who asks about not being companion to things. Gusu counters a monk claiming to have stepped clear, Mixing answers a question about the person within a local setting, and Minshu uses it when asked what is extraordinary. The same expanse overhead and underfoot leaves no privileged direction in which to search.

Senses.Explanation: The same unbroken expanse stretches above the head and beneath the feet. An appraisal verse places the line in the snow of Layman Pang's encounter; Jude Hongli makes the whiteness explicit in a snow address, while Baoning Renyong and Xiatang Huiyuan use the pair as direct answers. The Grove of the Mirror of the School preserves an unsigned verse on Pang's snow case that follows the pair with the difficulty of turning once planted. Jude Hongli opens ‘Good snow’ and locates it above and below. Baoning Renyong answers an interlocutor praising his lion's roar with it. Xiatang Huiyuan gives it when asked what to say about Danxia burning the wooden Buddha.

Senses.Note: A compiled case names Tong’an Changcha and preserves his answer to a monk asking what a teacher of gods and humans is: the horn is not fully grown and body hair has not emerged. Yichu Wuyuan quotes Tong’an’s answer and its two glosses, then composes his own verse on the unrecognized figure. Gulin Jiru quotes the same old exchange and adds a different verse about an ash-covered face, leisure, and rulers who cannot comprehend it. Tong’an remains the exact answer speaker in all three records; Yichu and Gulin are the later verse authors. Three independent contexts survive, so this reading is provisional.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB359.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baiyu. Baiyu Jingsi owns the retained deployment, finding after Layman Pang's verse that the two roads of lost and awake split the one power shared by sage and commoner, so that beings bob through the three worlds without rest.

Senses.Explanation: A fixed bobbing formula: the head comes up only to go under again, in the birth-and-death sea or wherever the turn plants it. Dongshan Shouchu sizes up those who lodge in the nameless realm as playing a tailless monkey in the stinking-water pit, bobbing till the year-end drum breaks and the monkey runs off, leaving them empty-handed, Dahui Zonggao counts his own years of seeking views and explanations as bobbing inside mind-consciousness, where the handed-down skeins of interpretation cannot quicken anyone, Yuanwu Keqin reads the beings in the karma sea as bobbing without knowing themselves, till Jizhi's one finger reaches them like the floating log reaching the blind turtle, and Qianyan Yuanzhang sizes up Yunmen as bobbing only in sound and color, where hearing a sound wakes the way and seeing a color lights the mind. Yuansou Xingduan traces the whirling wheel of birth and death to one mistaking of one's own mind, where every scene met becomes a clutching and every dust a seizing, Yongjue Yuanxian tells the mourning household that all beings sink in the birth-and-death sea, bobbing with no way out, from one deluded thought at the start, Yinyuan Longqi sets the founding teachers turning the great wheel on the tip of a hair and all beings bobbing on that same tip, too near for them to notice, and Baiyu Jingsi, after Layman Pang's verse of hauling water and carrying firewood, finds the one power and wonder shared by sage and commoner split by the two roads of lost and awake, so that beings bob through the three worlds without rest.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB305.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dayutao of Guoqing. Entries.SourceTerm: 頭長三尺知是誰，相對無言獨足立

Senses.PreferredTarget: Who has a head three feet long? Face to face and wordless, standing on one foot.
AlternateTargets: A three-foot head: who is it? Facing each other in silence, one foot planted
Senses.Note: Xuedou's paradoxical couplet closes a verse on Zhaozhou's warning against picking and choosing. Gulin quotes it to make his assembly investigate rather than guess; Haiyin later voices it in Master Zhou's memorial after a hawk-in-clouds image and a challenge to see clearly.

Occurrences.Kwic: ；趙州也如琢如磨，幾乎事不解交。眾中祇管道退身有分，殊不知盡力提持。還體悉麼？焦甎打著連底凍。雪竇頌云：至道無難，言端語端。一有多種，二無兩般。天際日上月下，檻前山深水寒。髑髏識盡喜何立，枯木龍吟消未乾。難難，揀擇明白君自看。隨庵緣云：世間無物可羅籠，獨立嵯峨萬仞峯。忽若有人猛推落，騰身雲外不留蹤。趙州僧問：至道無難，唯嫌揀擇。纔有語言是揀擇，和尚如何為人？師云：何不引盡這語？云：某甲祇念到這裏。師云：祇這至道無難，唯嫌揀擇。雪竇頌云：水灑不著，風吹不入。虎步龍行，鬼號神泣。頭長三尺知是誰，相對無言獨足立。白雲端云：驅山塞海也尋常，所至文明始是王。但見皇風成一片，不知何處有封疆。趙州，僧問：至道無難，唯嫌揀擇，是時人窠窟不？師云：曾有人問我，直得五年分疏不下。雪竇云：識語不能轉，死却了也，好與二十棒。這棒須有分付處，你若辨不出，且放此語。大行烏回範云：大眾！趙州具頂門眼，向擊石火裏分緇素，閃電光中明縱奪，為甚麼却五年分疎不下？還委悉麼？易分雪裏粉，難辨墨中煤。雪竇頌云：象王嚬呻，獅子哮吼。無味之談，塞斷人口。南北東西，烏飛兔走。白雲端云：分疏不下五年疆，一葉舟中載大唐。渺渺兀
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1299.xml). Classified Anthology of the Chan Grove. The anthology raises Zhaozhou's exchange with a monk who quotes the saying that the great way is not difficult if one avoids picking and choosing, yet asks how the master can speak without choosing. It then explicitly introduces Xuedou's verse, which moves through wind, water, tiger and dragon images before asking who has a head three feet long and stands on one foot without speaking face to face. The selected couplet is Xuedou's own verse on the Zhaozhou case, not Zhaozhou's answer or the questioning monk's words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 蝱弄空裏猛風，螻蟻撼於鐵柱。揀兮擇兮，當軒布鼓，一時裂破。雖然，也是箇斬釘截鐵漢始得。僧又問：至道無難，唯嫌揀擇。是時人窠窟否？州云：曾有人問我，直得五年分疎不下。好與掀倒禪床。雪竇頌云：象王回旋，獅子哮吼。無義之談，塞斷人口。南北東西，烏飛兔走。是什麼說話？也好與一拶。後又僧問：至道無難，唯嫌揀擇。才有語言是擇揀，和尚如何為人？州云：何不引盡者話？僧云：某甲只念到者裏。州云：只者便是至道無難，唯嫌揀擇。孟八郎漢又與麼去。雪竇和尚頌云：風吹不入，水洒不濕。虎步龍行，神號鬼泣。頭長三尺知是誰，相對無言獨足立。一對無孔鐵鎚，者般說話，諸人十二時中，還曾窮究也未？若未曾窮究，切忌向者裏東卜西卜。古人云：却物為上，逐物為下。是他本色道流，自然活鱍鱍地。豈肯將古人機緣，配在八識田中，自作障礙？雲門云：拈得便用，把得便撲。在今諸方覓箇舉話底，也難得好。兄弟，如斯理論，意在於何？只要你向古人未屙已前，千聖著眼不及處，坐斷報化佛頭，直是風凜凜地。山僧自來愛與兄弟東語西話，諸方聞得，往往謂之密室傳授。殊不知自有體裁，才見他開口，便知得他心肝五臟。何也？為他自己本分事上，不曾嗄地一聲，不能向古人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1412.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gulin Qingmao. Gulin Qingmao retells the Zhaozhou question about speaking without picking and choosing, then explicitly quotes Xuedou's verse, including the three-foot head and silent one-foot stance. Gulin calls the verses a pair of solid iron hammers and asks the assembly whether they have investigated them throughout the day; he warns against guessing here and there. Xuedou is the exact quoted speaker of the selected couplet, while Gulin is the current teacher pressing its practical investigation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 得。侍讀大學士員嶠、真逸總管相公，留意佛法，咨詢師友，欲得一道伴講明山中。今夏雖有百餘單，皆居學地，未可親近。大居士酬對拙謬，徑直寫數字，以當面言，萬冀親而求之，當必掀髯一咲。小佛事小佛事雪巖和尚忌日拈香雪巖和尚忌日拈香盡道先師今日死，不知今日是生朝。不知却有何憑據，紫栢黃檀一處燒。昔時語，今日舉，今昔一時，絕毫絕釐。大眾還見老和尚麼？插香凝立，云：面目現在，兩彩一賽。周禪師忌拈香周禪師忌拈香何似生，遼天鶻，萬重雲，只一突。者裡見得分明，便與祖師同起同倒，同放同収。其或未然，頭長三尺知是誰，相對無言獨足立。咄！瑛監寺入塔瑛監寺入塔用石牕燈盞，瑛瑛美玉無瑕；跨楊岐蹇驢，凜凜寒霜無影。正與麼時，如何明眼人落井？賢首座起骨賢首座起骨表帥叢林，山高水深。賢劫前事，只在如今。髑髏眼活老龍吟。轉身門外看，紅日上危岑。海印和尚語錄No.1398-B塔銘No.1398-B塔銘前集賢侍讀學士中大夫兩浙都轉運使河東李倜撰余來江右，以至元丁亥理事宜春，始識師于木平，式相好也。繼住慧力，余適守臨江，得顓意講道。居三年，往來至密。大德丁未，余調南劒，師來餞別豫章。無何，師亦往住薦福，音問不絕。嘗以古塔
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1398.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Haiyin Zhaoru. In the separate incense address for Master Zhou, Haiyin Zhaoru opens by asking what it is like, then pictures a hawk crossing layers of cloud in a single burst. He says that if one sees clearly here, one has not failed Zhou; otherwise he voices the three-foot-head and silent one-foot-stance couplet, then gives a sharp final exclamation. The selected words are Haiyin's present revoicing in Zhou's memorial address. The record does not locally introduce them as a quotation of Xuedou, though that older verse supplies a parallel origin.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Clear in every particular; understood in every thing.

Senses.Explanation: Clear in every particular; understood in every thing. The line names pervasive clarity, while masters test whether saying that settles the matter of seeing nature. One Tier-1 authored use and three distinct Tier-2 interpretive uses. Yuanwu describes full realization; Tianran sets it within his own exposition; Gulin Qingmao connects it to Zhaozhou; Weilin Daopei grants the claim and then challenges the distance it leaves. It is a claim about seeing in each circumstance, not an assertion that every object is separately enlightened.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Every part fits the track
Senses.Note: “Every part fits the track” pictures diverse acts finding a common course. Baichi says it when speaking of a world that appears everywhere; Baiyu pairs it with responses to different conditions. Feiyin and Wanru use it after a turn toward what is already present, and Yinyuan lets varied acts accord without fixing a single form. Shanyi cautions that simply declaring every part aligned may add another tangle of words. The line describes a living fit rather than a blanket approval of any reply.

Senses.Note: The two full spellings 子細 and 仔細 carry the same instruction to look closely at what each thing displays. Eight distinct Chinese Zen contexts are retained: an attributed verse, later commentaries and direct exchanges in which teachers or monks test whether that invitation has been understood.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1298.xml). Gāthās and Verses of the Chan Gate’s Patriarchs. In the series attributed to Fadeng, Qingliang Taiqin, imitating Hanshan, a poem asks who trusts the naturally present buddha. Knotweed, a white egret, dew on courtyard grass and a clearing moon lead to the closing injunction to look carefully at instruction offered everywhere. The poet speaks the pair directly: the landscape is the immediate occasion for attending, rather than a separate explanation of what must be recognized.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1304.xml). Elder Linquan’s Commentary and Chanted Remarks on Chan Master Danxia Zichun’s Verses on Ancient Cases: Xutang Collection. Linquan Conglun comments on Danxia's verse about the complete, dignified form already possessed by everyone. He warns against abandoning this inheritance to pursue appearances, then asks whether his listeners recognize what he has just laid out. He closes with the pair as his own direct challenge. The words turn his explanation back onto present recognition; Danxia is the earlier verse author, not the speaker of this closing cap.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1359.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Ying’an Tanhua. During Ying'an Tanhua's evening gathering, an unnamed monk asks about Maitreya and receives the rough answer, "What dried dung-stick?" The monk then offers the pair about instruction everywhere and careful observation. Ying'an replies, "You have no buddha-nature; what are you observing?" The monk is the exact speaker of the pair. Ying'an's reversal prevents the familiar invitation to observe from serving as an untested answer to the Maitreya question.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1998A.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue. An unnamed monk asks Dahui Zonggao whether Deshan's entrance blows and Linji's entrance shouts are the same or different. After several exchanges, the monk offers the pair about instruction everywhere and looking carefully. Dahui says he spares him thirty blows, then addresses the assembly against arranging and contriving. The monk, rather than Dahui, voices the inherited injunction. Its use here is tested within an actual exchange about the teachers' gestures, rather than accepted as a sufficient interpretation.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1298.xml). Gāthās and Verses of the Chan Gate’s Patriarchs. In the series attributed to Fadeng, Qingliang Taiqin, imitating Hanshan, a poem asks who trusts the naturally present buddha. Knotweed, a white egret, dew on courtyard grass and a clearing moon lead to the closing injunction to look carefully at instruction offered everywhere. The poet speaks the pair directly: the landscape is the immediate occasion for attending, rather than a separate explanation of what must be recognized.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1304.xml). Elder Linquan’s Commentary and Chanted Remarks on Chan Master Danxia Zichun’s Verses on Ancient Cases: Xutang Collection. Linquan Conglun comments on Danxia's verse about the complete, dignified form already possessed by everyone. He warns against abandoning this inheritance to pursue appearances, then asks whether his listeners recognize what he has just laid out. He closes with the pair as his own direct challenge. Senses.Note: The phrase says that every encountered thing is the Way. Feiyin points to autumn flowers and says it becomes so when understood; without understanding the same person remains lost. Wuyi puts it after a turn away from seeking an image elsewhere. Baichi says the line over birdsong and flowers, then immediately warns that such speech can deceive a novice. Konggu places it after a long instruction in looking directly. Chushi contrasts seeing the root with confusion amid the same surroundings. Yuanwu speaks it in a sermon where many differences meet in one response. The saying depends on the listener actually recognizing what is encountered.

Senses.Explanation: Every particular encountered thing may disclose the Way, but the words alone do not accomplish that seeing. Feiyin, Wuyi, and Baichi place the saying beside recognition and the risk of an easy claim. Konggu, Chushi, and Yuanwu use it after investigation, in direct counsel, and in a sermon on varied conditions.

Entries.SourceTerm: 頭頭非取捨，處處沒張乖

Senses.PreferredTarget: At every point, neither grasp nor reject; anywhere, no forced opposition
AlternateTargets: Nothing to seize or discard in each thing, no quarrel to contrive anywhere
SearchAliases: neither grasp nor reject no forced opposition
Senses.Note: In Pang Yun’s verse on daily activity, “at every point neither grasp nor reject; in every place do not force a quarrel” describes an ordinary action that needs no contrived division. Feiyin quotes the full verse but presses beyond making its plainness into a possession; Miyun uses the pair in a letter against splitting delusion from religious aspiration; Tianyin questions how Pang could speak a verse after saying daily activity left him no words; Changming turns water carrying and wood gathering into a present test; Pingshi brings the verse into dressing, eating, and ordinary work. Five distinct uses make the inherited line concrete.

Occurrences.Kwic: 侍者火。雙弘定慧，兼善毗尼。生死岸頭，了無交涉。擲下火。犀牛扇子足清風，火裡蝍蟟吞大虫。上堂：清霜鋪大野，白月滿空山，目前明歷歷，一點不相瞞。擊拂子，下座。宏智和尚忌日拈香。夢幻空花，六十七年。白鳥煙沒，秋水天連。渾侖無縫罅竇，八布衫穿。丹霞室內，太白峰前。正偏俱不涉，生死不相干。夜行只管貪明月，不覺和衣渡水寒。冬至，小參。佛法二字也是不著，便衲僧家從朝至暮著衣喫飯、痾屎送尿，何甞有虗棄底時節？豈不見龐居士頌云：日用事無別，惟吾自偶諧，頭頭非取捨，處處沒張乖。朱紫誰為號？丘山絕點埃，神通并妙用，運水及搬柴。諸仁者，看他是箇俗流，宛有衲僧氣息，若向者裡著得一隻眼，觀風雲、別氣候，觸目遇緣、隨機應變，灼然無虗曇底時節；苟或未然，且向陰陽消長處一任東卜西卜。復舉：洞山冬夜與泰首座喫果子次，問云：有一物黑似漆，常在動用中，動用中收不得，過在什麼處？泰首座云：過在動用中。洞山令侍者掇退果卓。師云：泰首座恁麼答話，本分不得果子喫。雖然，洞山也不得無過，即今若有人下一轉語，坐斷古人舌頭，天童向明窓下安排

Senses.Explanation: “At every point, neither grasp nor reject; anywhere, no forced opposition” is Pang Yun’s line about daily activity. Feiyin presses beyond treating Pang’s plainness as a possession, Miyun applies the verse in a letter, and Tianyin asks how a verse could follow Pang’s claim that daily activity leaves no words. Changming tests the line through carrying water and wood; Pingshi brings it into dressing, eating, and ordinary response.

Senses.Explanation: Each thing openly reveals it: Chan speakers use this phrase to direct attention to what shows itself in every particular of the present scene. Baichi Xingyuan pairs disclosure in every particular with completion in every thing, then asks listeners to act from that seeing. Zhulang Chesheng says the constant is disclosed in each thing, naming birds, water, and mountains in the same address. Minshu Ruxiang links each disclosure to fully raising the command, then returns to wearing robes and carrying the bowl. Xiuye Minglin's verse says speech and silence both show it without concealment. Ruibai Mingxue says that even when one wants to cast the matter aside, it appears in every particular. Dabian Xianquan describes the spring scene as disclosing its original purity in each thing. Hanxiu Ruqian says opening one's eyes reveals it in every particular, bringing incense, fire, and work into the scene.

Senses.Explanation: The head officers are the monastery's senior west-rank officers. One regulation names the category's offices—chief seat, secretary, librarian, guest prefect, and bath prefect—and prescribes how they are invited and escorted into their quarters. Other rules make them lead the assembly and forbid the assembly from taking position before them; public addresses distinguish them from the stewards while calling both groups to act.
